text:
**Short answer:** for a typical full-size fridge, get a pure sine wave power station with about 1,300 W or more of surge output and 1,000 Wh for most of a day. For a full 24 hours, or a margin of safety, aim for 1,500-2,000 Wh. For two days, plan on about 2,800 Wh.

## The three numbers to check

1. **Surge watts (the one that most often blocks a fridge).** The compressor spikes on startup, roughly 1,000-2,400 W depending on fridge size. Look for a surge rating of at least 1,300 W, and more for a large French-door or older fridge ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage), [powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).
2. **Continuous watts.** Most fridges run at about 100-250 W, which almost any 1,000 W-class station covers ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)). Add any other devices you'll run at the same time.
3. **Watt-hours.** The compressor only runs about 30-40% of the time, so the average draw is much lower than the label wattage. Estimates range from about 41 W average ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)) to 60-70 W ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)). That works out to roughly 1,000-1,700 Wh per day once you allow for inverter losses and headroom.

Also look for a **pure sine wave** inverter, since compressor motors can run hot or fail to start on cheap modified sine units.

## Get a better number for your fridge
- Check the yellow EnergyGuide label: kWh/year × 1,000 ÷ 8,760 = average watts ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).
- Or look up your model in the DOE's refrigerator energy rating tool, or measure it with a plug-in energy meter ([iTechGuides](https://www.itechguides.com/how-to-size-a-portable-power-station-for-a-refrigerator-and-essential-devices/)).
- Large side-by-sides with ice makers can use about twice the average of an efficient top-freezer. Hot rooms and frequent door openings also raise use.

## Options that fit

| Most of a day | [BLUETTI AC180](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage) | 1,152 Wh, 1,800 W (2,700 W peak) | ~$399-699 |
| 24+ hours | [BLUETTI AC200L](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac200l) | 2,048 Wh, 2,400 W | ~33 hrs, $899 ($854.05 with code AFF5OFF) |
| 24+ hours | [Anker SOLIX S2000](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator) | 2,010 Wh, 1,500 W (3,000 W peak) | $699.99 after coupon |

The runtimes come from HomeGridHQ's estimate, which assumes a 35% duty cycle and 85% inverter efficiency. Real runtime will vary. The AC200L link is an affiliate link, and prices and availability change, so confirm at checkout.

## Practical tips
- Keep the door closed. The USDA says food becomes unsafe after about 4 hours above 40°F with the door shut ([HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)).
- Test the setup before an outage.
- For multi-day outages, choose an expandable unit or add solar. The AC200L expands to 8,192 Wh.

If you tell me your fridge's size or model, how long an outage you want to cover, and what else you'd plug in (CPAP, router, freezer), I can narrow this to one pick.
